sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Minimally invasive image-guided ablation therapies are emerging as alternatives for lung cancer and metastatic lung tumors in patients who are not surgical candidates. Modalities include radiofrequency ablation (RFA), microwave ablation (MWA), cryoablation, laser ablation, and irreversible electroporation (IRE).

rows.Radiofrequency ablation: Uses electrical currents at 375–500 kHz to generate heat through resistive energy loss
rows.Microwave ablation: Applies electromagnetic fields (900–2500 MHz) to agitate water molecules, generating heat
rows.Cryoablation: Delivers pressurized gas through a cryoprobe, creating extreme cold via the Joule–Thomson effect
rows.Laser ablation: Delivers heat from a neodymium-doped yttrium aluminum garnet (Nd:YAG) laser emitting 1064 nm light
rows.Irreversible electroporation: Uses electrical pulses (microseconds to milliseconds) to create permanent nanopores in cell membranes

rows.Radiofrequency ablation: Small- to medium-sized tumors (<3 cm). May use cooling or infusion to enhance efficacy
rows.Microwave ablation: Suitable for larger tumors (3–5 cm or more)
rows.Cryoablation: Useful for lesions near critical structures. Various freeze–thaw–freeze cycles. Probes placed no more than 2 cm apart
rows.Laser ablation: Primarily for small, accessible lung lesions. The smallest access size
rows.Irreversible electroporation: Effective for tumors near critical structures
Variable; depends on tumor size and complexity

rows.Radiofrequency ablation: Tumors not close to major blood vessels or airways due to potential heat-sink effect
rows.Microwave ablation: Effective for difficult-to-reach locations, peripheral preferred to avoid central harm
rows.Cryoablation: Anywhere. Safe near vital structures such as airways, blood vessels, and bones
rows.Laser ablation: Accessible small peripheral lesions in the lung
rows.Irreversible electroporation: Okay near critical structures; less suitable for tumors with significant necrosis or calcification

rows.Cryoablation: 25–28 min per cycle; generally longer than RFA or MWA
rows.Irreversible electroporation: 20–60 min depending on tumor size and complexity

rows.Radiofrequency ablation: Well-established with FDA approval. Low risk of complications. Shorter recovery
rows.Microwave ablation: Can treat larger tumors, faster ablation, larger ablation zone, not limited by conductive paths
rows.Cryoablation: Ice ball visualization, minimal collateral damage, lower risk of bronchopleural fistula, less pain
rows.Laser ablation: Precise control with thin applicators, potentially lower procedural costs
rows.Irreversible electroporation: Nonthermal; preserves vessels and matrix, may enhance immune response

rows.Radiofrequency ablation: Less effective for large tumors or near critical structures. Interference with pacemakers
rows.Microwave ablation: Higher risk of collateral damage due to broader heat zone; device design variability
rows.Laser ablation: Tissue charring may impair effectiveness. Limited long-term outcome data
rows.Irreversible electroporation: Not effective for tumors with necrosis/calcification. Long-term outcomes under investigation

rows.Indication: Early-stage lung cancer in nonsurgical candidates
rows.Special consideration: Preserves pulmonary function with favorable outcomes
Localized control, potential long-term remission if all sites treated
rows.Contraindication: Tumor proximity to critical structures (unless cryoablation)

rows.Special consideration: Useful in patients with limited pulmonary reserve from prior treatments

rows.Indication: Combination therapy with surgery or radiation

rows.Special consideration: Targets progressing lesions to prolong survival
rows.Contraindication: Severe COPD, pulmonary fibrosis, or emphysema
